The approach every project follows

Each folder is a small research paper in code form. The mathematics is written out with every step shown, the code mirrors the equations line for line, and a test file checks the implementation against something that is known to be true: a theorem, a closed-form answer, or a trusted library.

1 · Derive

Start from a definition and reach the algorithm with pen and paper. Every formula in the project's write-up has its steps shown.

2 · Worked example

A problem small enough to check by hand. Two-by-two matrices, five data points, one training step.

3 · Implement

Pure NumPy. Functions, not frameworks. Immutable parameters so every step returns a new object.

4 · Verify

Tests that encode theorems, not just behaviour. Finite differences, LAPACK, conservation laws, closed-form posteriors.

5 · Apply

Real data where it exists: MNIST, a 1978 influenza outbreak, Hubble's 1929 measurements. Then write down what surprised me.

01

Neural network from scratch

Complete
chain rulematrix calculusgradient descent softmax & cross-entropyfinite differencesHe initialisation

A two-layer network that reads handwritten digits, written with nothing but NumPy. The point is not the accuracy. The point is that the backward pass is derived, not copied, and then proven correct two independent ways.

1The model

An image is a row vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^{784}$. The network is two affine maps with a ReLU between them and a softmax at the end:

$$ \begin{aligned} Z_1 &= X W_1 + b_1 &\quad& (n \times 128) \\ A_1 &= \operatorname{ReLU}(Z_1) = \max(0, Z_1) \\ Z_2 &= A_1 W_2 + b_2 &\quad& (n \times 10) \\ P &= \operatorname{softmax}(Z_2), \qquad P_{ij} = \frac{e^{Z_{2,ij}}}{\sum_{k} e^{Z_{2,ik}}} \end{aligned} $$

The loss is the average cross-entropy between the predicted distribution and the one-hot label $Y$:

$$ L = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{10} Y_{ij} \log P_{ij} $$

2The derivation

Backpropagation is the chain rule applied layer by layer, from the loss back to the inputs. Three results carry the whole thing.

Softmax + cross-entropy collapse

Differentiating the loss with respect to the logits, the softmax Jacobian and the log cancel almost entirely:

$$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial Z_2} = \frac{1}{n}\,(P - Y) $$

Predicted minus true, divided by batch size. This is why the pair is used together.

Dense layer, three gradients

For $Z = XW + b$ with upstream gradient $G = \partial L / \partial Z$:

$$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W} = X^{\mathsf T} G, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T} G, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial X} = G\, W^{\mathsf T} $$

Shapes check themselves: $(784 \times n)(n \times 128) = 784 \times 128$, the shape of $W_1$.

ReLU is a gate

$$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial Z_1} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial A_1} \odot \mathbf{1}[Z_1 > 0] $$

Gradient flows through the units that were active and is blocked at the ones that were not.

One step of gradient descent

$$ \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\, \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} $$

With $\eta = 0.1$ and mini-batches of 64 images. He initialisation $W \sim \mathcal N\!\left(0, \tfrac{2}{\text{fan}_{\text{in}}}\right)$ keeps the ReLU activations from collapsing.

3Worked example you can check by hand

A 2-2-2 network with one input $x = [1, 2]$, label $y = [0, 1]$, and

$$ W_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0.1 & -0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad W_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & -0.5 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad b_1 = b_2 = 0 $$

4Verification

A derivation can be wrong in ways that still train. Two independent checks close that gap.

Central finite differences

Nudge one parameter up and down and measure the loss change. The central formula has error $O(h^2)$:

$$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_k} \approx \frac{L(\theta + h e_k) - L(\theta - h e_k)}{2h} $$

With $h = 10^{-5}$, every entry of $W_1, b_1, W_2, b_2$ agrees with the analytic gradient to relative tolerance $10^{-5}$.

PyTorch autograd

The same forward pass written in Torch, gradients taken by autograd. Maximum absolute disagreement with the hand-derived gradient:

$$ \max_k \left| g_k^{\text{mine}} - g_k^{\text{torch}} \right| < 10^{-10} $$

Torch is used only here, in the tests. It never touches the model.

5Results on MNIST

EpochTrain lossTest lossTest accuracy
10.29170.212293.76 %
50.06740.104096.85 %
Lesson learned: 100× from one environment variable The first training run took 25 minutes. Profiling showed each 64 × 784 batch multiply taking 0.32 s, while the 10 000-row test-set pass took 0.03 s. NumPy's multithreaded BLAS was spending its time coordinating threads on matrices too small to split. Setting OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 before importing NumPy dropped the run to 24 seconds with identical results. Small matrices want one thread.
Lesson learned: two numerical guards Softmax overflows for logits above about 709, so the maximum is subtracted from each row first. The result is mathematically identical because the shift cancels in the ratio. And $\log(0)$ is $-\infty$, so cross-entropy clips probabilities at $10^{-12}$.
02

Principal component analysis from scratch

Complete
eigenvaluesLagrange multipliersspectral theorem power iterationSVDnumerical stability

PCA finds the directions along which data varies most. Most tutorials call an eigensolver and stop. Here the eigensolver is written by hand, and the reason PCA is an eigenproblem is derived rather than asserted.

1The idea in one picture

2The derivation: why eigenvectors?

Centre the data so each column has mean zero, and form the sample covariance matrix:

$$ C = \frac{1}{n-1} X_c^{\mathsf T} X_c \qquad (d \times d,\ \text{symmetric},\ \text{positive semi-definite}) $$

The variance of the data projected onto a unit vector $u$ is $u^{\mathsf T} C u$. We want the $u$ that maximises it, subject to $\lVert u \rVert = 1$. A Lagrange multiplier turns the constrained problem into an unconstrained one:

$$ \mathcal L(u, \lambda) = u^{\mathsf T} C u - \lambda\,(u^{\mathsf T} u - 1), \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal L}{\partial u} = 2 C u - 2 \lambda u = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; C u = \lambda u $$

So every critical point is an eigenvector, and the variance there is $u^{\mathsf T} C u = u^{\mathsf T} (\lambda u) = \lambda$. The largest variance is the largest eigenvalue. Three consequences follow from the spectral theorem $C = \sum_i \lambda_i u_i u_i^{\mathsf T}$:

Total variance is the trace

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{d} \lambda_i = \operatorname{tr}(C) $$

So "fraction of variance explained" by component $i$ is simply $\lambda_i / \operatorname{tr}(C)$.

Reconstruction error is the dropped eigenvalues

$$ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \lVert x_j - \hat x_j^{(k)} \rVert^2 = \frac{n-1}{n} \sum_{i > k} \lambda_i $$

Keep $k$ components and the mean squared error is exactly what was left out.

Same answer as the SVD

$$ X_c = U \Sigma V^{\mathsf T} \;\Longrightarrow\; C = V \frac{\Sigma^2}{n-1} V^{\mathsf T}, \qquad \lambda_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1} $$

The right singular vectors of the centred data are the principal components.

3The hand-written eigensolver

Power iteration: multiply a random vector by $C$, rescale to unit length, repeat. Writing $v_0 = \sum_i c_i u_i$ in the eigenbasis,

$$ C^{t} v_0 = \sum_i c_i \lambda_i^{t} u_i = \lambda_1^{t} \left( c_1 u_1 + \sum_{i \ge 2} c_i \left(\tfrac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_1}\right)^{t} u_i \right) $$

Every term but the first shrinks geometrically, at rate $\lambda_2 / \lambda_1$. Once $u_1$ and $\lambda_1$ are found, deflation removes them and the next eigenpair becomes dominant:

$$ C' = C - \lambda_1 u_1 u_1^{\mathsf T} $$

4Worked example you can check by hand

Five points in the plane: $(2,1), (3,3), (4,3), (5,5), (6,5)$. Mean $[4, 3.4]$. Covariance and its characteristic polynomial:

$$ C = \begin{bmatrix} 2.5 & 2.5 \\ 2.5 & 2.8 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \det(C - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 - 5.3\lambda + 0.75 = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \lambda_1 = 5.1545,\ \lambda_2 = 0.1455 $$

60 000 images, 784 pixels each. The first 100 components were computed with the hand-written solver in about 66 seconds.

Components $k$Variance explainedReconstruction MSE
19.7 %47.608

An observation from the data The covariance matrix has rank 712, not 784. Seventy-two border pixels are black in every single image, so those directions have variance exactly zero. Any method that divides by eigenvalues, like whitening, needs a guard for this.
Lesson learned: deflation loses orthogonality Textbook deflation says the removed direction now has eigenvalue zero, so it should never come back. In floating point it does: each multiply reintroduces a component of about $10^{-16}$ along it, and for slowly converging eigenpairs those grow to $10^{-5}$. The fix is one Gram–Schmidt sweep per iteration against the eigenvectors already found. The tests caught this; the mathematics alone would not have.
Lesson learned: choose the stopping rule from the geometry Stopping when successive iterates agree, $1 - |v_{t+1} \cdot v_t| < 10^{-12}$, plateaued at $10^{-8}$ accuracy. The reason is that $1 - \cos\theta \approx \theta^2 / 2$, which hits machine epsilon while $\theta$ is still $10^{-8}$. Switching to the residual $\lVert C v - \lambda v \rVert \le 10^{-12} |\lambda|$, which is linear in the angle, fixed it.
03

SIR epidemic model with Runge–Kutta

Complete
ordinary differential equationsRunge–Kutta 4order of convergence conservation lawsNelder–Meadparameter fitting

The first project outside machine learning. A population is split into Susceptible, Infected, and Recovered, and three coupled differential equations describe how people move between the groups. There is no closed-form solution, so the equations are solved with a Runge–Kutta integrator I wrote, then fitted to a real outbreak with a Nelder–Mead optimiser I also wrote. NumPy arrays are the only library code in the implementation; SciPy appears once, inside a test, as the reference solver.

1The model

$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{dS}{dt} &= -\beta \frac{S I}{N} \\[4pt] \frac{dI}{dt} &= \beta \frac{S I}{N} - \gamma I \\[4pt] \frac{dR}{dt} &= \gamma I \end{aligned} \qquad\qquad R_0 = \frac{\beta}{\gamma} $$

$\beta$ is the contact rate, $\gamma$ the recovery rate, and $R_0$ the number of people one infected person infects in a fully susceptible population. Writing $dI/dt = I(\beta S/N - \gamma)$ shows the outbreak grows if and only if $R_0 > 1$, and that infections peak exactly when $S = N / R_0$.

2The solver

Euler's method takes a step along the current slope. Runge–Kutta 4 samples the slope four times per step and averages them with weights $1, 2, 2, 1$:

$$ \begin{aligned} k_1 &= f(t_n, y_n) \\ k_2 &= f\!\left(t_n + \tfrac{h}{2},\ y_n + \tfrac{h}{2} k_1\right) \\ k_3 &= f\!\left(t_n + \tfrac{h}{2},\ y_n + \tfrac{h}{2} k_2\right) \\ k_4 &= f(t_n + h,\ y_n + h k_3) \\ y_{n+1} &= y_n + \frac{h}{6}\,(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4) \end{aligned} $$

The global error is $O(h^4)$: halve the step and the error should drop by a factor of 16. That is a testable claim, and the convergence-order test measures it.

3Worked example you can check by hand

$N = 1000$, one infected person, $\beta = 0.5$ and $\gamma = 0.25$ per day, so $R_0 = 2$. One RK4 step of one day:

5Results: influenza in a boarding school, 1978

A letter to the British Medical Journal (4 March 1978) reported an outbreak among 763 boys at a boarding school in the north of England. One boy returned from holiday infected; the letter lists how many were confined to bed each day for two weeks. A closed population with one index case and daily counts is as close to the SIR assumptions as real data gets.

QuantityFitted / predictedObserved
$\beta$, $\gamma$1.665, 0.448 per day
$R_0 = \beta / \gamma$3.723.6 to 3.8 in the literature
Peak289 boys on day 6.4291 boys on day 6
Final size743 boys (97 %)512 confined to bed (67 %)
What the numbers say The peak fits well; the final size does not. Boys with mild cases were never sent to bed, so "in bed" undercounts the infected on the way down, which is why the last four data points sit below the curve. The counterfactual is "flatten the curve" as a consequence of the final-size relation: with $R_0$ near 3, intervention buys a lower, later peak rather than fewer total infections.
Lesson learned: the fitted $R_0$ depends on a number the data does not contain The fit assumes one index case. Assuming 0.5, 2, 3 or 5 gives $R_0$ between 3.28 and 3.91, because a bigger seed needs a slower disease to reach 291 by day 6. The honest statement is "$R_0 \approx 3.7$ given one index case", with 3.3 to 3.9 as a better summary of the uncertainty than any single number.
Lesson learned: Nelder–Mead is local From three different starting guesses the simplex found $R_0 = 3.72$. From $(\beta, \gamma) = (10, 0.2)$ it ran off to a fit eighty times worse and still reported success, because the error surface there is nearly flat. Gradient-free does not mean global.
Lesson learned: conservation is a necessary check, not a sufficient one With a step of two days, Euler's method produced $-1.6 \times 10^7$ infected boys while $S + I + R$ still equalled 763 to $10^{-9}$. Any method built from linear combinations of the right-hand side conserves the total, however wrong the parts are. The non-negativity test catches what the conservation test cannot.
04

Markov chain Monte Carlo from scratch

Complete
Bayes' theoremMarkov chainsdetailed balance Metropolis–Hastingsconvergence diagnosticsuncertainty

Bayesian inference says the posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. The trouble is the constant of proportionality, an integral that is usually impossible. MCMC sidesteps it: build a random walk whose long-run distribution is the posterior, then let it walk. The sampler, the diagnostics and the models are NumPy; SciPy appears only in the tests.

1The goal

$$ p(\theta \mid D) = \frac{p(D \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)}{\displaystyle\int p(D \mid \theta')\, p(\theta')\, d\theta'} \;\propto\; p(D \mid \theta)\, p(\theta) $$

Only the numerator ever needs to be evaluated. The denominator cancels in everything that follows.

2The algorithm and why it works

From the current point $\theta$, propose $\theta' \sim q(\theta' \mid \theta)$, here a Gaussian step. Accept it with probability

$$ \alpha(\theta \to \theta') = \min\!\left(1,\ \frac{p(\theta' \mid D)\, q(\theta \mid \theta')}{p(\theta \mid D)\, q(\theta' \mid \theta)}\right) $$

Otherwise stay put. The acceptance rule is chosen so the chain satisfies detailed balance, $\pi_i P_{ij} = \pi_j P_{ji}$ for every pair of states. Detailed balance implies the target is stationary. Sum the identity over $i$:

$$ \sum_i \pi_i P_{ij} = \sum_i \pi_j P_{ji} = \pi_j \sum_i P_{ji} = \pi_j \qquad \blacksquare $$

So running the chain one step from $\pi$ leaves it at $\pi$. With a Gaussian random walk on a target with positive density, the chain also converges to $\pi$ from any start.

3Verification: twenty-nine tests

Test groupWhat it checks
Detailed balance (5)on an explicit three-state transition matrix: rows sum to one, $\pi_i P_{ij} = \pi_j P_{ji}$ exactly, $\pi P = \pi$, and the hand calculation matches
Beta–Binomial coin (5)the posterior is known in closed form, so its mean, variance and quantiles are checked against SciPy
Metropolis sampler (6)recovers the mean and variance of a standard Gaussian and the covariance of a correlated 2-D Gaussian; sensible acceptance rate; reproducible for a fixed seed
Diagnostics (5)autocorrelation time of an AR(1) process with a known answer; $\hat R \approx 1$ for agreeing chains and flagged for disagreeing ones
Regression (4)posterior mean matches ordinary least squares; log densities match the direct formula

Hubble's 1929 data. Edwin Hubble's original table of 24 galaxies, distance against recession velocity. The slope is the Hubble constant $H_0$. Four chains of 20,000 kept steps each, from scattered starting points:

ParameterLeast squaresPosterior mean95 % interval$\hat R$
$H_0$, km/s per Mpc454.2452.7$[294.5,\ 614.3]$1.0023
Intercept, km/s$-40.8$$-39.3$$[-217.8,\ 136.8]$1.0024
What the numbers say The posterior mean agrees with least squares, but the posterior also shows what least squares does not: with 24 points, the data support any slope from roughly 300 to 600. Hubble's value is about seven times the modern value of about 70. The reason is not statistical: his distances were systematically too small. The posterior faithfully reports the uncertainty in the data it was given; it cannot know the data are biased.
Lesson learned: work in log space, always The posterior density at the best fit is around $10^{-62}$. A data set ten times larger would underflow to exactly zero and turn every acceptance ratio into $0/0$. Logarithms turn products into sums and keep every number ordinary.
Lesson learned: 80,000 samples were worth about 3,000 Successive samples are correlated; the integrated autocorrelation time for the slope was 28. The honest sample size is $n / \tau$, and every reported uncertainty has to use it. Skipping this step is the most common way to overstate the precision of an MCMC result.
Lesson learned: the step size has a sweet spot A step of $0.1\sigma$ accepted 95 % of proposals and went nowhere; a step of $40\sigma$ accepted 3 % and stood still between rare jumps. The efficient middle is around $2.4\sigma$ in one dimension and shrinks as $2.4/\sqrt{d}$. The three-parameter Hubble run landed at an acceptance rate of 0.236, close to the theoretical 0.23.
05

Fast Fourier transform from scratch

Complete
complex numbersroots of unitydivide and conquer Parseval's theoremconvolution theoremsignal processing

The Fourier transform rewrites a signal as a sum of sines and cosines. Computing it from the definition costs $O(N^2)$. The FFT does it in $O(N \log N)$ by a piece of algebra so clean it is often called the most important algorithm of the twentieth century. I implemented it twice, recursively and iteratively, in pure NumPy, then used it to read the notes off a chord, denoise it, and draw a spectrogram. numpy.fft appears only in the tests.

1The definition

$$ X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n\, e^{-2\pi i\, kn / N}, \qquad k = 0, \dots, N-1 $$

Each $X_k$ measures how much of the frequency $k$ is present in $x$. Written as a matrix, this is $N$ dot products of length $N$.

2The trick

Split the sum into even-indexed and odd-indexed terms. With $\omega = e^{-2\pi i / N}$,

$$ X_k = \underbrace{\sum_{m} x_{2m}\, \omega^{2mk}}_{E_k} \;+\; \omega^{k} \underbrace{\sum_{m} x_{2m+1}\, \omega^{2mk}}_{O_k} $$

$E_k$ and $O_k$ are themselves Fourier transforms of length $N/2$. And because $\omega^{k + N/2} = -\omega^k$, one pair of half-size transforms gives two outputs:

$$ X_k = E_k + \omega^k O_k, \qquad X_{k + N/2} = E_k - \omega^k O_k $$

Recursing gives the cost $T(N) = 2\,T(N/2) + O(N)$, which solves to $O(N \log N)$. For one second of audio that is about 700,000 multiplications instead of two billion.

3Verification: seventy-eight tests

TestCriterionTolerance

4Results

Reading the notes off a chord. A synthesised A-major chord (A4, C♯5, E5) with harmonics, two seconds at 44.1 kHz. The three loudest peaks in the spectrum are the three notes, at 440.08, 554.48 and 659.12 Hz, each within one frequency bin (0.34 Hz) of the truth. The harmonics fall exactly where they should, and the 3rd harmonic of A4 lands on the 2nd harmonic of E5, which is why A and E sound consonant together.

Denoising. White noise is added at equal power to the signal (0 dB signal-to-noise). Zeroing every frequency bin above 2 kHz and transforming back raises it to 10.45 dB. The prediction: white noise spreads evenly over 22,050 Hz, so keeping 2,000 Hz keeps 9.1 % of it, a gain of 10.4 dB.

Speed. At $N = 16\,384$ the naive sum takes 4.5 seconds; the iterative FFT takes 2.15 milliseconds, 2,000 times faster.

Lesson learned: a ninth peak that is not a note The peak finder reported a small peak at 424 Hz, labelled G♯4, though there is no G♯ in the chord. Zero-padding a finite signal multiplies it by a rectangle, and the spectrum of a rectangle is a sinc with sidelobes on either side of every true peak. Tapering with a window removes them; the spectrogram does exactly this, and its lines are clean.
Lesson learned: recursion loses to the naive sum below about $N = 512$ A recursive FFT of length $N$ makes $2N - 1$ Python function calls, each costing microseconds regardless of how little arithmetic it does. The iterative version does $\log_2 N$ vectorised stages with no function calls and wins at every size. The asymptotic argument is right, but constants decide who wins on small inputs.
Lesson learned: brick-wall filters ring Zeroing every bin above a cutoff multiplies the spectrum by a rectangle, which by the convolution theorem convolves the signal with a sinc. Near any sharp change, the filtered output oscillates. The chord survives untouched only because all of its components sit well below the cutoff.

Running the projects

Each project is its own GitHub repository. Python 3.11 or newer. PyTorch is used only to download MNIST in projects 01 and 02 and to check gradients in project 01's tests. SciPy appears only inside the tests of projects 03 to 05.

# Setup, once per project (shown for project 01)
git clone https://github.com/hrithikponduru-ops/01-neural-network-from-scratch.git
cd 01-neural-network-from-scratch
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Project 01: neural network
python -m pytest tests/ -v        # 5 gradient tests
python worked_example.py          # the 2-2-2 example, every number printed
python train.py                   # 5 epochs, about 25 seconds

# Project 02: PCA (inside 02-Principal-Component-Analysis-From-Scratch)
python -m pytest tests/ -v        # 9 theorem tests
python worked_example.py          # the five-point example
python run.py                     # MNIST, about 1 minute

# Project 03: SIR epidemic model (inside 03-SIR-epidemic-model)
python -m pytest tests/ -v        # 12 tests
python worked_example.py          # one RK4 step and the final size, by hand
python run.py                     # fit to the 1978 outbreak, figures

# Project 04: MCMC (inside 04-Markov-Chain-Monte-Carlo-From-Scratch)
python -m pytest tests/ -v        # 29 tests, about 15 seconds
python worked_example.py          # three Metropolis steps on a coin
python run.py                     # coin check and Hubble regression, about 5 seconds

# Project 05: FFT (inside 05-fft-From-Scratch)
python -m pytest tests/ -v        # 78 tests, about 7 seconds
python worked_example.py          # a length-8 FFT by hand
python run.py                     # chord, denoising, spectrogram, timing; about 20 seconds

Each repository contains a write-up with the full derivations, the code map, and the figures shown on this page.
